rv.q: So let’s be clear: Decouflé, Takahashi and team have done a bang-up job in both putting the stranger bits of this novel on stage, but also turning it all into a fairly digestible story. Ultimately it’s less moving than the book, and the final few sections get bogged down frantically tying up loose ends.
But that was Complicité, famous for reaching parts of the human psyche that other theatre companies couldn’t. Surely this theatrical sleight of hand couldn’t be pulled off again.

Watashi (Tatsuya Fujiwara demonstrates an unexpected gift for comedy) works as a data-encryption specialist called a Calcutec in a dystopian Tokyo, rendered in a stark palette of noirish monochrome, impressionistic back projections, and gloomy shadows by set designer K Ishihara and lighting designer Yukiko Yoshimoto.

Two parallel stories run side by side, occasionally touching each other and resolving - well, as much as any Murakami work does - by the end. We open on a Japanese warrior with a horn that is bigger than he is, surrounded by unicorns, ballet dancers en pointe making a remarkable facsimile of the mythical creatures.

And Decouflé certainly doesn’t skimp on ingredients. There’s brilliant acting, breathtaking choreography, beautiful live music and sumptuous stage and sound design. The result is a sensory spectacle that feels perfectly Murakami: dreamlike, dazzling and totally different to anything you’ve seen before.
